name: Spinal dural arteriovenous fistula
aliases: dural AV fistula of the spine

reference.source: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: This is the commonest spinal vascular malformation and characteristically affects middle-aged and older men, most often at thoracolumbar levels
The lesion is an acquired arteriovenous shunt within the dura of a nerve root sleeve, where a radiculomeningeal artery drains directly into a radicular vein and arterialises the coronal venous plexus
The resulting venous hypertension impairs cord drainage and produces a progressive congestive myelopathy rather than haemorrhage
Patients present with insidious, often stepwise, ascending paraparesis, sensory disturbance and sphincter dysfunction that can be mistaken for a degenerative or inflammatory process
Symptoms characteristically worsen with exertion, prolonged standing, heat or the Valsalva manoeuvre, reflecting the underlying venous congestion
MRI typically shows central cord T2 hyperintensity with cord swelling and serpentine flow voids on the dorsal cord surface, and often patchy enhancement
Catheter spinal digital subtraction angiography remains the gold standard to localise the fistulous point before treatment
The advanced, thrombotic and often irreversible form is known as the Foix-Alajouanine syndrome
reference.pathophysiology: A spinal dural arteriovenous fistula is an acquired direct shunt situated in the dura near a spinal nerve root, where a dural branch of a radiculomeningeal artery connects to a radicular (medullary) vein without an intervening capillary bed. Arterial pressure is transmitted into the normally low-pressure, valveless coronal venous plexus that drains the cord, raising spinal venous pressure and reducing the arteriovenous pressure gradient. The consequent failure of venous drainage causes chronic venous congestion, interstitial oedema and cord hypoxia, producing a progressive myelopathy; unlike intramedullary arteriovenous malformations, the low-flow dural shunt rarely bleeds, and superimposed venous thrombosis can precipitate abrupt, often irreversible deterioration.
additionalDifferentials: Transverse myelitis and other inflammatory myelopathies
Intramedullary spinal cord tumour such as ependymoma or astrocytoma
Intramedullary arteriovenous malformation or perimedullary fistula
Subacute combined degeneration of the cord
Motor neurone disease when weakness predominates
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the whole spine with contrast to show cord oedema, dorsal serpentine flow voids and enhancement
MR angiography of the spine to help localise the level of the shunt
Catheter digital subtraction spinal angiography as the definitive study to identify the feeding artery and fistulous point
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis, which may show a mildly raised protein, to help exclude inflammatory causes
Serum vitamin B12 and metabolic screen to exclude mimics of a progressive myelopathy
Baseline functional and bladder assessment to monitor response to treatment
redFlags: Progressive gait decline with exertional or postural worsening in an older man
Ascending sensory level with developing sphincter involvement
Abrupt deterioration suggesting venous thrombosis or the Foix-Alajouanine syndrome
reference.prognosis: Gait and motor function commonly improve after treatment by endovascular embolisation or surgical ligation, provided intervention occurs before fixed deficits develop, whereas sphincter recovery is less reliable. Delayed diagnosis allows irreversible cord injury and can result in permanent paraplegia.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the condition as transverse myelitis and giving corticosteroids, which may precipitate marked deterioration
Overlooking the dorsal serpentine flow voids on MRI that signal the diagnosis
Failing to proceed to spinal angiography when imaging suggests a vascular myelopathy
Attributing progressive myelopathy to degenerative spinal disease and missing a treatable fistula
Not recognising exertional and postural symptom fluctuation as a clue to venous congestion
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
Osborn's Diagnostic Imaging: Brain and Spine
